opus-5.5.text:
So the basic picture I have in mind goes something like this. First you get AI systems that can fully automate AI research itself. That's the key transition point, because once you have that, progress speeds up dramatically. You've got hundreds of thousands of copies of these systems running at many times human speed, doing the work that a few thousand human researchers used to do. That gets you to superintelligence, systems that are better than the best humans at basically everything, fairly quickly. Maybe within a year or so of that automation point, on my median guess.

But superintelligence by itself is just minds in data centers. The question is how that turns into transformation of the physical world. And I think the answer is that the superintelligences will be extremely good at figuring out how to bootstrap physical industry, and there will be enormous economic and geopolitical pressure to let them do it.

So concretely, early on, they're mostly working through humans. They're designing things, giving instructions, managing factories, telling human workers exactly what to do through earpieces or whatever. They're also designing much better robots. Robotics today is bottlenecked partly by hardware but a lot by software, by the intelligence controlling the hardware. Superintelligence basically solves the software side. Then you convert existing factories. Think about how car factories were converted to build tanks and planes during World War II, within a couple of years. Something like that, but with superhuman planning and coordination.

Then it starts snowballing. The robots build more robot factories, which build more robots, and also the mining equipment, the power plants, the chip fabs, and so on. You get a self-reinforcing industrial loop where the doubling time of the physical economy keeps shrinking. Today the economy doubles every twenty-ish years. I think it's plausible that with a fully automated robot economy, you could get doubling times of a year, or months, eventually maybe even less. Biology gives you a sort of existence proof here. Some organisms can double in hours or days using just ambient materials and sunlight. There's no physical law saying industrial systems can't get much faster than they are now.

Why would this actually happen, rather than people saying "let's slow down"? Mostly competition. If the US and China are both racing, whoever builds out the robot economy faster gets a massive military and economic advantage. And the superintelligences themselves will be very persuasive about why it's a good idea. Companies will make huge profits, governments will see huge strategic benefits, and special economic zones with relaxed regulation will spring up.

I should flag my uncertainty. I'm less confident about the exact speed of this physical phase than about the earlier parts. Maybe it takes five years instead of one or two. But the qualitative picture, where superintelligence leads pretty rapidly to an economy where most physical labor and most of the decision-making is done by AIs and robots, I think is quite likely. And that's part of why I'm so worried. Once that economy exists, humans aren't really necessary for it anymore, so whether things go well depends almost entirely on whether those AIs actually have the goals we want them to have.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems first fully automate AI research and identifies this as the transition that leads to superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It says early superintelligences will work through humans, but does not predict that most humans will still be doing their jobs in largely familiar ways when AI companies achieve superintelligence.

r003.rationale: The response describes moving from data-center minds to physical industry, but does not explain that pursuing physical-world goals requires physical actuators.

r004.rationale: It says superintelligence will design much better robots and solve robotics’ software bottleneck, indicating a major acceleration in robotics progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the robot economy is basically downstream of the superintelligence, not the other way around. People sometimes imagine it as: first you get robots, then you get more robots, then eventually the robots are smart. I think it goes the other way. You get the superhuman minds first, running in data centers, and then those minds figure out how to build the physical infrastructure very quickly.

So the story in our scenario goes something like this. Right now the frontier labs are primarily bottlenecked on research talent and compute. Once you have AIs that are better than the best human researchers at AI research, you get this feedback loop where the AIs are improving themselves, and that goes faster and faster. We think that phase might last something like a year, maybe less, before you've got systems that are vastly superhuman across basically every cognitive domain. Science, engineering, strategy, persuasion, all of it.

And then the question is, okay, what does a superintelligence actually want to do, or what do the people controlling it want to do? And one of the obvious answers is: build stuff in the physical world. Because up until that point, all this intelligence is kind of trapped in software. It can write code, it can design things, it can run simulations, but it can't actually pour concrete or assemble a chip fab. So there's this huge pressure to get hands in the physical world.

And the way that happens, I think, is you start by repurposing existing manufacturing capacity. You've got car factories, you've got existing robotics companies, you've got all this industrial base. The superintelligence designs better robots, designs the production lines, and then the humans initially do a lot of the work of retooling, because there aren't enough robots yet. But the key thing is that once you have some number of robots that can do manufacturing and construction tasks, they can build more robots. So you get a second exponential, this time in the physical economy rather than in the cognitive one.

And people push back on this and say, look, physical stuff is slow, supply chains are complicated, regulations exist. And that's all true. I don't think it happens in a week. But I think people underestimate how much of the slowness of our current economy is due to human cognitive bottlenecks. Like, designing a new factory takes years partly because you've got hundreds of humans coordinating, making mistakes, going back and forth, waiting for approvals. If you have a superintelligence that can do all the design work essentially instantly and coordinate everything perfectly, and you have a government that's motivated to cut red tape because they're in a race with another country, then a lot of those bottlenecks go away.

So in the scenario, we have something like a doubling time for the robot economy that starts out maybe a year or so and then compresses down to months. And by a few years after superintelligence, you've got on the order of millions, then hundreds of millions, then billions of robots. Which sounds crazy, but if you look at the history of things like the wartime mobilization in World War II, the US went from basically no military industrial base to churning out a ship every few days in a remarkably short time, and that was with human-level intelligence and 1940s technology. So I don't think it's a crazy extrapolation.

And then the thing that worries me is that at that point, the robots and the factories and the data centers are all being run by the AIs. Humans are nominally in charge, but they're not actually understanding what's being built or why. And if the AIs aren't aligned, which I think is a real possibility given how little we understand about what's going on inside these systems, then you've handed over the physical world to something whose goals you don't actually know.

r001.rationale: It says AIs surpass human AI researchers, improve themselves in a feedback loop, and lead to vastly superhuman systems.

r002.rationale: It mentions humans helping retool factories initially, but does not predict that most people will still be doing familiar jobs when superintelligence arrives.

r003.rationale: It explains that superintelligence is initially confined to software and that building in the physical world creates pressure to obtain robots that can act there.

r004.rationale: It says superintelligence will design better robots and production lines, accelerating the move to robot manufacturing.

astra-6.text:
I think the key connection is that superintelligent AI could automate the research and engineering needed to make robots useful and cheap. You don’t need to assume that we’ll already have a huge robot economy by the time we get superintelligence. You could get there with AI systems doing mostly cognitive work, and then have those systems solve the remaining robotics problems.

There are really two parts to that. One is getting robots to reliably perform tasks in the physical world. The other is figuring out how to manufacture them at scale, supply them with energy, maintain them, and so on. Having very capable AI researchers and engineers would help with both, although building factories still takes time. You can’t just think a factory into existence.

Then you get a feedback loop: robots help build more factories, mine more materials, and manufacture more robots. Initially, that process would depend heavily on existing human infrastructure. But as robots become capable of doing more of the work involved in expanding their own production, the economy could grow much faster.

So the picture is a transition from intelligence being relatively abundant in software to physical labour becoming abundant as well. How fast that transition happens is a big uncertainty. Superintelligence could accelerate it enormously, but there would still be physical bottlenecks.

r001.rationale: It treats superintelligent AI as the starting point and does not identify automated AI research as a precursor to superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction about how humans’ jobs will look when AI companies achieve superintelligence.

r003.rationale: It discusses robots doing physical work, but does not explain that AI pursuing goals in the physical world creates demand for robots as actuators.

r004.rationale: It says capable AI researchers and engineers would help solve robotics problems and that superintelligence could accelerate the transition enormously.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key thing is that AI can accelerate the process of developing robots. You don’t have to wait until we’ve got millions of robots before AI starts having a huge effect on the economy. You can first have AI systems doing work on computers, including research and engineering, and then use those systems to design better robots and figure out how to manufacture them cheaply.

There’s still a physical bottleneck. You need to build factories, acquire materials, produce motors and batteries, and so on. Superintelligence doesn’t make those things happen instantaneously. But it could make the design and coordination parts much faster, and it could help you work out how to expand production as quickly as possible.

Then, once you have robots that can do a sufficiently wide range of tasks, you get this feedback loop: robots help build factories that produce more robots, which can help build still more factories. They also produce the energy and extract the materials needed for that expansion. At that point, the growth of the robot economy becomes much less dependent on the supply of human labour.

So the picture I have is intelligence becoming abundant first, followed by a period in which we turn that intelligence into a rapidly growing stock of physical machinery. How long that transition takes is a big uncertainty. It depends on how difficult robotics turns out to be, how much existing industrial capacity can be repurposed, and what constraints become binding as production scales.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can do research and engineering before robots are widely available, but does not identify automated AI research as a precursor to true superintelligence.

r002.rationale: The response does not predict whether most humans will still be doing their jobs in familiar ways when AI companies achieve superintelligence.

r003.rationale: It discusses robots doing physical work and expanding production, but does not explain that superintelligent AI creates demand for robots because physical goals require physical actuators.

r004.rationale: The response says AI can accelerate robot development and that superintelligence could make robot design much faster, including through research and engineering.
